open.text: Here's a little shop's orders table. Every row has a key, nothing's null... every constraint passes.

twice.text: But look closer. Ada's email is stored twice, and so is the notebook's price.

rushed.text: So Ada changes her email, and a rushed update fixes only order one. Postgres says, update one. No complaints.

disagree.text: Now Ada has two emails. No constraint broke... the design let one fact live in two places.

siblings.text: That's the update anomaly, and it has two siblings.

insert.text: Add a mug nobody's ordered yet? Refused, because every row here has to be an order.

delete.text: And when Grace cancels her only order, deleting it deletes Grace too.

home.text: The cure is one rule. Every fact gets exactly one home.

tables.text: Customers get a table, products get a table, and each order just points at both.

once.text: Now Ada's email is one row to change, the mug can wait for its first order, and Grace outlives hers.

join.text: Need the wide view back? A join rebuilds it, any time.

forms-in.text: Normal forms get you there in steps, starting with what fits in a cell.

cell.text: First normal form means one value per cell. Here's Ada, with two phone numbers in one.

search.text: Ask who has five five five, twenty-two hundred... and Postgres finds nobody. It's buried in a string.

columns.text: Phone one, two and three instead? That's a repeating group, with a ceiling. A fourth number won't fit.

child.text: The fix is a child table. Each number gets its own row, pointing back at its student.

plain.text: Now a search is a plain equals, Linus can have none at all, and a unique constraint stops Ada's number going in twice.

depend-in.text: So each cell holds one value. But what does each value depend on?

pair.text: Second normal form is about keys with two parts, like this pair: order and product.

whole.text: Quantity needs the whole pair. Order one hundred took two notebooks, order one oh one took one.

part.text: But the product name only needs half. Product ten is Notebook on every order.

partial.text: That's a partial dependency. It copies the name onto every line, so a rename changes two rows.

move.text: So the name moves to products, and a rename is one row.

chain-in.text: Third normal form catches something sneakier.

chain.text: These orders carry each customer's city. The key is the order ID... but a city isn't about an ORDER. It's about the customer.

detour.text: Order ID gives you customer ID, which gives you the city. A dependency with a detour: transitive.

moves.text: Same disease. Ada moves to Oxford, the update misses a row, and she lives in two cities.

extract.text: Give customers their own table, and she moves exactly once.

oath.text: There's an old oath for this. Every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

halves.text: The whole key is second normal form. Nothing but the key is third.

kent.text: William Kent put it that way in nineteen eighty-three. Somebody later added... so help me Codd.

denorm-in.text: So should every table stay normalized forever? Almost.

summary.text: Say a report keeps asking what sold each day. You could store the answer, in a summary table.

days.text: Two orders on January tenth, thirty-two fifty. One on the eleventh, twelve dollars.

denorm.text: That's denormalization. Duplicating on purpose, so a read gets simpler.

stale.text: But add four dollars to that last order, and the summary still says twelve. It's gone stale.

sync.text: So every copy needs a sync plan, and a clear source of truth.

prices.text: And some copies aren't copies. Northwind stores a price on each product, and another on every order line.

history.text: Six hundred sixty-two lines disagree, and they're RIGHT. Prices rose, and each line kept what the customer paid.

facts.text: Two facts that share a name. A copy needs syncing. History needs nobody to ever fix it.

rule.text: So, normalize first, denormalize on purpose, and keep every copy in sync.

next.text: Knowing the rules is half of it. The other half is a process for using them, and for changing a design once it's live.
